notes: First-refresh audit, 2026-09-01. Every epidemiological statistic in the pre-audit article was absent from its own cited NCI page and from every stored source; the whole "Research Gap" and "Why Non-Smoking Women" sections were rebuilt from H. Rept. 119-382, SEER, CDC and USPSTF. Removed outright (no source exists): the breast/ovarian/cervical-combined mortality comparison; the 20%-of-women vs 10%-of-men never-smoker split; the "under 50" claim; the EGFR/ALK/ROS1 vs p53/KRAS mechanism sentence; the male-study-population history; "a growing share of lung cancer cases"; "Congress frequently passes such bills as a precursor to larger legislation"; and the study-and-report-bills-often-stall generalisation.

claims.claim: The bill directs HHS, with Defense and Veterans Affairs, to review federal research on lung cancer in women and underserved populations
claims.sourceSpan: The Secretary of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, shall conduct an interagency review

claims.claim: The report is due to Congress within two years
claims.sourceSpan: Not later than two years after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall submit to Congress a report on the review conducted under subsection (a).

claims.claim: The House Energy and Commerce Committee report on the bill is H. Rept. 119-382
claims.sourceSpan: Committee reports: H. Rept. 119-382

claims.claim: The committee report states that lung cancer is the third most common cancer in the United States
claims.sourceSpan: Lung cancer is the third most common cancer in the United States.

claims.claim: The committee report states that worldwide, over 600,000 women die of lung cancer each year
claims.sourceSpan: Worldwide, over 600,000 women die of lung cancer each year.

claims.claim: The committee report states that about 10 to 20 percent of lung cancers, or 20,000 to 40,000 a year, occur in people who never smoked or smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes
claims.sourceSpan: About 10 to 20 percent of lung cancers, or 20,000 to 40,000 lung cancers each year, happen in people who never smoked or smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lifetime.

claims.claim: The committee footnoted the CDC for the first and third of those figures
claims.sourceSpan: Lung Cancer Statistics, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

claims.claim: The committee footnoted the Lung Cancer Research Foundation for the 600,000 figure
claims.sourceSpan: Women and Lung Cancer, Lung Cancer Research Foundation

claims.claim: CDC states that more people in the United States die from lung cancer than any other type of cancer, and that this is true for both men and women
claims.sourceSpan: More people in the United States die from lung cancer than any other type of cancer. This is true for both men and women.

claims.claim: NCI SEER records lung and bronchus cancer as the first leading cause of cancer death in the United States
claims.sourceSpan: Lung and bronchus cancer is the first leading cause of cancer death in the United States.

claims.claim: SEER estimates 124,990 lung and bronchus cancer deaths in 2026
claims.sourceSpan: Estimated Deaths in 2026 124,990

claims.claim: That is 20.0% of all cancer deaths
claims.sourceSpan: % of All Cancer Deaths 20.0%

claims.claim: The five-year relative survival rate is 29.5%
claims.sourceSpan: 5-Year Relative Survival 29.5%

claims.claim: The 29.5% survival figure covers cases diagnosed in 2016-2022
claims.sourceSpan: 5-Year Relative Survival 29.5% 2016–2022

claims.claim: The SEER death rates are age-adjusted and based on 2020-2024 deaths
claims.sourceSpan: The death rate was 30.2 per 100,000 men and women per year based on 2020–2024 deaths, age-adjusted.

claims.claim: The age-adjusted death rate is 35.4 per 100,000 men
claims.sourceSpan: Death Rate per 100,000 Persons by Race/Ethnicity & Sex: Lung and Bronchus Cancer Males All Races 35.4

claims.claim: The age-adjusted death rate is 26.2 per 100,000 women
claims.sourceSpan: Females All Races 26.2 Hispanic 10.8

claims.claim: The SEER incidence rates are age-adjusted and based on 2019-2023 cases
claims.sourceSpan: The rate of new cases of lung and bronchus cancer was 47.2 per 100,000 men and women per year based on 2019–2023 cases, age-adjusted.

claims.claim: The rate of new cases is 52.0 per 100,000 men
claims.sourceSpan: Rate of New Cases per 100,000 Persons by Race/Ethnicity & Sex: Lung and Bronchus Cancer Males All Races 52.0

claims.claim: The rate of new cases is 43.6 per 100,000 women
claims.sourceSpan: Females All Races 43.6 Hispanic 23.2

claims.claim: The committee says the bill would help advance both existing research and emerging opportunities needed to reduce lung cancer mortality
claims.sourceSpan: would help advance both existing research and emerging opportunities needed to reduce lung cancer mortality

claims.claim: The committee frames that aim as especially concerning women, who face unique risks and outcomes
claims.sourceSpan: who face unique risks and outcomes

claims.claim: Section 2(a) directs the Secretary of HHS to act in consultation with the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs
claims.sourceSpan: in consultation with the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs

claims.claim: The first research area is research on lung cancer in women
claims.sourceSpan: research on lung cancer in women;

claims.claim: The second research area is research on lung cancer in underserved populations that meet the USPSTF lung cancer screening eligibility criteria
claims.sourceSpan: research on lung cancer in underserved populations that meet the eligibility criteria for lung cancer screening as recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force

claims.claim: The third research area is access to lung cancer preventive services
claims.sourceSpan: access to lung cancer preventive services

claims.claim: The fourth research area is strategic public awareness and education campaigns on lung cancer
claims.sourceSpan: strategic public awareness and education campaigns on lung cancer

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(1) requires a review and comprehensive report on prior research outcomes, existing activity and knowledge gaps in all agencies of the Federal Government
claims.sourceSpan: a review and comprehensive report on the outcomes of previous research, the status of existing research activities, and knowledge gaps related to lung cancer in women and underserved populations in all agencies of the Federal Government

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(2)(A) covers innovative approaches to eliminate knowledge gaps in research on lung cancer in women
claims.sourceSpan: encourage innovative approaches to eliminate knowledge gaps in research on lung cancer in women

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(2)(B) covers evaluating environmental and genomic factors related to the etiology of lung cancer in women
claims.sourceSpan: evaluate environmental and genomic factors that may be related to the etiology of lung cancer in women

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(2)(C) covers advances in imaging technology to improve risk assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and the simultaneous utilization of other preventive services and activities
claims.sourceSpan: foster advances in imaging technology and techniques to improve risk assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and the simultaneous utilization of other preventive services and activities

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(3) covers opportunities to develop a national lung cancer screening strategy expanding access, particularly among women and underserved populations
claims.sourceSpan: a national lung cancer screening strategy to expand access to such screenings, particularly among women and underserved populations

claims.claim: Section 2(b)(4) covers a national public education and awareness campaign including the importance of early detection
claims.sourceSpan: the importance of early detection of lung cancer

claims.claim: Section 2(c) requires the report to Congress not later than two years after enactment
claims.sourceSpan: Not later than two years after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall submit to Congress a report on the review conducted under subsection (a).

claims.claim: The reach of the review is set by the phrase "in all agencies of the Federal Government"
claims.sourceSpan: in all agencies of the Federal Government

claims.claim: The USPSTF appears once in the bill, only as the source of the screening criteria that define one of the four research areas; only HHS, Defense and Veterans Affairs are given a role in the review
claims.sourceSpan: research on lung cancer in underserved populations that meet the eligibility criteria for lung cancer screening as recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force

claims.claim: The committee found the bill would result in no new or increased budget authority, entitlement authority, or tax expenditures or revenues
claims.sourceSpan: would result in no new or increased budget authority, entitlement authority, or tax expenditures or revenues

claims.claim: The committee report records that the legislation does not amend any existing Federal statute
claims.sourceSpan: This legislation does not amend any existing Federal statute.

claims.claim: The bill is a study-and-report directive, not a funding or program authorization - the committee states its general performance goal as reviewing, evaluating and identifying research and educational opportunities
claims.sourceSpan: the general performance goal or objective of this legislation is to review, evaluate the status of, and identify research and educational opportunities related to lung cancer in women and certain underserved populations

claims.claim: The committee report closes its background statement by saying a better understanding of risk factors beyond smoking is needed, particularly around women and underserved populations
claims.sourceSpan: A better understanding of additional risk factors beyond smoking cigarettes is needed for more effective screening, diagnosis, treatment, and public health strategies, particularly around women and underserved populations.

claims.claim: The USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT screening for adults aged 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years
claims.sourceSpan: recommends annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) in adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years

claims.claim: The USPSTF lung cancer screening recommendation carries a grade of B
claims.sourceSpan: Grade: B

claims.claim: The Task Force expanded the age range from 55-80 to 50-80 and cut the pack-year threshold from 30 to 20
claims.sourceSpan: It expanded the age range to 50 to 80 years (previously 55 to 80 years), and reduced the pack-year history to 20 pack-years of smoking (previously 30 pack-years).

claims.claim: USPSTF eligibility is defined by age and smoking history, so a person who never smoked does not meet the criteria
claims.sourceSpan: Adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years

claims.claim: The committee report puts the never-smoker share at about 10 to 20 percent of lung cancers
claims.sourceSpan: About 10 to 20 percent of lung cancers

claims.claim: NCI states that smoking causes most lung cancers but that nonsmokers can also develop lung cancer
claims.sourceSpan: Smoking causes most lung cancers, but nonsmokers can also develop lung cancer.
